{\LARGE\bfseries\sffamily\color{AtlasNavy} Stochastic smooth convex minimization: convexity on a ball and heavy-tailed centered noise; stochastic full gradients\par}\vspace{5pt}


\textbf{Setting ID.} \texttt{SO\_\allowbreak{}FO\_\allowbreak{}S02\_\allowbreak{}cv\_\allowbreak{}alpha}



Single-objective optimization



Find an approximate global minimizer, with accuracy measured by suboptimality of the complete objective.



\textbf{Status.} Other quantified gap present



\textbf{TASK tags.} formulation: Global minimization; task family: Single objective



\textbf{MODEL tags.} convexity: Convex; geometry: Euclidean ball; geometry: Full space; smoothness: Lipschitz gradient; stochastic model: Centered alpha moment noise



\textbf{ORACLE tags.} access order: First-order interface; feedback quality: Stochastic; interface family: Stochastic gradient; operation: Stochastic gradient; public information: Hidden objects explicitly declared; public information: Known upper bound; public information: Known exact value; public information: Public inputs explicitly declared



\textbf{ALGORITHMS tags.} adaptivity: Adaptive; computation: Internal arithmetic uncharged; randomization: Deterministic algorithms; randomization: Private randomness allowed; restriction: No additional span restriction explicitly imposed



\textbf{OUTPUT tags.} certificate: No additional output certificate required; feasibility: Required; object: Point; postprocessing: Unqueried output explicitly allowed



\textbf{METRIC tags.} criterion: Objective gap

\textbf{RESOURCE tags.} budget: Fixed worst-case budget; measure: Samples; precision: Bit precision not counted



\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{1. Setting specification}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Task}


Find an approximate global minimizer, with accuracy measured by suboptimality of the complete objective.




\AtlasMath{\min_{x\in Q}f(x)}




\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Admissible model}


The unknown function \AtlasInlineMath{f} is convex and \AtlasInlineMath{\beta}-smooth on the public ball \AtlasInlineMath{Q}, whose prox diameter is finite. This differs from an unrestricted unconstrained initial-distance model.



Feasible geometry: \AtlasInlineMath{Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|x\|_2\le R\}}.



Unless another geometry is specified, vectors use the Euclidean norm \AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_2}, and matrices and higher derivatives use the corresponding operator norm. The assumptions hold uniformly throughout the declared domain.



Here \AtlasInlineMath{\beta}-smoothness means \AtlasInlineMath{\|\nabla f(u)-\nabla f(v)\|_2\le\beta\|u-v\|_2} for all \AtlasInlineMath{u,v} in the declared model domain.



Admissible parameter domain:


\AtlasMath{\begin{gathered}\varepsilon > 0,\quad d \ge 1,\quad \varepsilon \le c\,\beta\,{R}^{2},\quad \beta > 0\\\sigma \ge 0,\quad \alpha > 1,\quad \alpha \le 2,\quad R > 0\end{gathered}}




\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Oracle interface}


Public numerical inputs: \AtlasInlineMath{d,\ \alpha,\ \varepsilon}.



Public upper bounds: \AtlasInlineMath{\beta,\ R,\ \sigma}.



The unknown object is the objective \AtlasInlineMath{f}.



Query points lie in \AtlasInlineMath{Q}; feedback consists of stochastic full gradients:




\AtlasMath{\mathbb{E}_tG_t=\nabla f(x_t),\quad\mathbb{E}_t\|G_t-\nabla f(x_t)\|^\alpha\le\sigma^\alpha}




Every observation is fresh. Same-point batches are conditionally independent, and the conditional moment bounds hold uniformly over histories. Samples cannot be reused across points.



Exact Euclidean projection onto the public domain; its internal computation is free



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Output}


Return a point \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat x\in Q}.



The output may be unqueried or constructed from the query history, provided it is feasible. No additional function value or accuracy certificate is required.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Loss or accuracy criterion}



\AtlasMath{\ell(I,\widehat{x})=f(\widehat{x})-f^\star}




\AtlasInlineMath{f^\star=\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)}. The existence, compactness, or initial-suboptimality assumptions ensure that the optimal value in this comparison is finite.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Resource accounting}


One full stochastic-gradient sample costs one call; a batch of \AtlasInlineMath{b} samples costs \AtlasInlineMath{b} calls.



Cost is bounded uniformly on every execution path. All calls used for initialization, repetition, batching, or candidate verification are counted.



Real arithmetic, precision, and storage applied to already available information are uncharged. Public geometric operations are limited to those explicitly granted by the oracle. Query complexity alone does not imply arithmetic, memory, or communication complexity.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Algorithm views and success guarantees}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Deterministic / Expected loss}


The algorithm uses no private random numbers. Query and stopping decisions may depend adaptively on the observed feedback.



No additional span, zero-respecting, linear-iteration, or memory restriction is imposed.



Interaction is adaptive to the feedback history. Every actual response is charged separately, including responses in parallel or batch queries. Internal real arithmetic, storage, and postprocessing are uncharged.



Select an algorithm using the public parameters, and then require the following for every admissible instance and response rule:




\AtlasMath{\forall I\,\forall\mathcal{O}\in\mathcal{O}(I):\ \mathbb{E}_{A,\mathcal{O}}\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le\varepsilon}




The probability space includes observation noise. The algorithm uses no private random numbers. The instance and its admissible oracle law are fixed before randomness is averaged.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Randomized / Expected loss}


Private randomization is allowed. Queries, stopping decisions, and postprocessing may adapt to observed feedback.



No additional span, zero-respecting, linear-iteration, or memory restriction is imposed.



Interaction is adaptive to the feedback history. Every actual response is charged separately, including responses in parallel or batch queries. Internal real arithmetic, storage, and postprocessing are uncharged.



Select an algorithm using the public parameters, and then require the following for every admissible instance and response rule:




\AtlasMath{\forall I\,\forall\mathcal{O}\in\mathcal{O}(I):\ \mathbb{E}_{A,\mathcal{O}}\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le\varepsilon}




The probability space includes observation noise and the algorithm's private randomness. The instance and its admissible oracle law are fixed before randomness is averaged.



\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{2. Notation and parameters}


\AtlasInlineMath{x,\widehat{x}}: Query points and final output; their permitted spaces are specified separately by the oracle and output contracts \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{x}\in Q}.



\AtlasInlineMath{f}: Unknown objective, with domain and structure specified by the model



\AtlasInlineMath{\nabla f}: Full gradient of the differentiable objective or smooth term with respect to the decision variable



\AtlasInlineMath{f^\star}: Optimal value of the complete task; the oracle need not return it




\AtlasMath{f^\star=\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)}




\AtlasInlineMath{Q}: Feasible set of the task




\AtlasMath{Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|x\|_2\le R\}}




\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d}: Real vector space with \AtlasInlineMath{d} coordinates



\AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_2,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle}: Euclidean norm and inner product



\AtlasInlineMath{G_t}: \AtlasInlineMath{t}th full stochastic gradient or subgradient observation



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{E}_t}: Conditional expectation given the previous history and current query; the query is selected before the fresh observation is drawn



\AtlasInlineMath{d}: Ambient dimension; a positive integer tracked explicitly. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\beta}: Public upper bound on the gradient smoothness constant. Any mean-square interpretation is specified in the model. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\beta>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mu}: Lower bound on the strong-convexity modulus of the objective specified by the model \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\mu>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{R}: Radius of the public feasible ball \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{R>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\Delta}: Public upper bound on initial suboptimality. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\Delta>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\sigma}: Public upper bound on the scale of the conditional centered noise moment. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\sigma\ge0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\alpha}: Order of the centered noise moment. Every bound with a subscripted constant treats this order as fixed; uniformity as it approaches one is not asserted. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{1<\alpha\le2}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}: Target tolerance for the underlying error defined by the accuracy measure \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{c}: Sufficiently small universal positive constant, potentially different between theorems; it is not a numerical threshold. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<c<1}.



\AtlasInlineMath{C}: Sufficiently large universal constant, independent of the tracked parameters; no numerical value is specified. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{C>1}.



\AtlasInlineMath{S}: Number of halving stages, \AtlasInlineMath{\max\{1,\lceil\log_2(2\Delta/\epsilon)\rceil\}}.




\AtlasMath{S=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2(2\Delta/\varepsilon)\rceil\}}




\AtlasInlineMath{V}: Heavy-tailed statistical term at the final accuracy scale.




\AtlasMath{V={\frac{{\sigma}^{2}}{\mu\,\varepsilon}}^{\frac{\alpha}{2\,((\alpha-1))}}}




\AtlasInlineMath{c_\alpha}: Positive multiplicative constant depending only on the fixed \AtlasInlineMath{\alpha}; uniform boundedness as \AtlasInlineMath{\alpha\downarrow1} is not asserted. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<c_\alpha<\infty}.



\AtlasInlineMath{C_\alpha}: Positive multiplicative constant depending only on the fixed \AtlasInlineMath{\alpha}; uniform boundedness as \AtlasInlineMath{\alpha\downarrow1} is not asserted. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<C_\alpha<\infty}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\ell}: The underlying loss or error defined by the accuracy measure; its expected, probabilistic, or worst-case aggregation is specified by the success contract



\AtlasInlineMath{I,\mathcal{O},A}: Admissible instance, a response rule consistent with that instance, and an algorithm; the algorithm is selected before the unknown instance



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{E}}: Expectation over the declared randomness after fixing the instance and admissible response law



\AtlasInlineMath{O,\Omega,\Theta,\widetilde{O},\widetilde\Omega}: Notation for asymptotic upper and lower bounds, constant-factor matching rates, and explicitly permitted logarithmic factors. Hidden-constant dependence is specified in each regime.



\AtlasInlineMath{\log}: Natural logarithm; changing to another fixed base affects only a constant

\textbf{Oracle correspondence.} Applicable interfaces: stochastic full gradients. Lower bounds transfer only through the explicitly recorded simulations from a stronger interface to a weaker one.



\textbf{Guarantee conversion.} The hard-instance quantifiers cover the algorithm class explicitly specified for this bound. Each target setting retains its expected-error or success-probability criterion; a deterministic lower bound is not promoted to a randomized lower bound.



\textbf{Output rule.} The output must lie in the declared output space and satisfy its feasibility, support, or atomic-hull restrictions. Permission to return an unqueried point does not remove these restrictions.



\textbf{Resource conversion.} Every primitive response is charged. Sample, component, proximal, and communication costs use the units declared for the target setting. Resource coordinates achieved by one algorithm remain a joint vector; coordinatewise minima from different algorithms are not combined.

A hidden sign determines mean \$\textbackslash{}pm a\$. Return zero with probability \$1\char45{}\textbackslash{}pi\$, and \$\textbackslash{}pm a/\textbackslash{}pi\$ with probability \$\textbackslash{}pi\$. This is unbiased, with
\$\textbackslash{}mathbb E|Y\char45{}\textbackslash{}mathbb EY|\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}le C\_\textbackslash{}alpha a\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}pi\textasciicircum{}\{1\char45{}\textbackslash{}alpha\}\$.
Choose \$\textbackslash{}pi\$ proportional to \$(a/\textbackslash{}sigma)\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}alpha/(\textbackslash{}alpha\char45{}1)\}\$ when it is below a fixed constant. If \$T\textbackslash{}pi\textbackslash{}le c\$, all observations are zero with constant probability, leaving the signs indistinguishable even for adaptive randomized algorithms.

For convex optimization on \$[\char45{}R,R]\$, take \$f\_\textbackslash{}pm(x)=\textbackslash{}pm ax\$, \$a=C\textbackslash{}epsilon/R\textbackslash{}le L\$. On the common transcript, the two instances\char39{} average loss is \$aR\$, giving
\$\textbackslash{}Omega\_\textbackslash{}alpha((\textbackslash{}sigma R/\textbackslash{}epsilon)\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}alpha/(\textbackslash{}alpha\char45{}1)\})\$.

For strong convexity, use \$f\_\textbackslash{}pm(x)=\textbackslash{}mu x\textasciicircum{}2/2\textbackslash{}mp ax\$, with response \$\textbackslash{}mu x\char45{}Y\$, and \$a=C\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}epsilon\}\$. The recorded window \$\textbackslash{}epsilon\textbackslash{}le c\textbackslash{}mu R\textasciicircum{}2\$ keeps both minimizers in the domain. On the common transcript, average loss is at least \$a\textasciicircum{}2/(2\textbackslash{}mu)\$, giving
\$\$
\textbackslash{}Omega\_\textbackslash{}alpha((\textbackslash{}sigma\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}epsilon))\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}alpha/[\allowbreak{}2(\textbackslash{}alpha\char45{}1)]\}).
\$\$
For the Lipschitz model, continue convexly with bounded slopes outside the query domain. For the global smooth strongly convex model the quadratics already qualify. At \$\textbackslash{}alpha=2\$, these are the finite\char45{}variance terms.

The noise parameter here is centered, not a total\char45{}gradient moment. Exact function values are not part of this lower\char45{}bound interface. A statistical expression below a constant supplies no additional nontrivial query obstruction.

The noise\char45{}free subclass remains admissible for any noise upper bound. In the stated high\char45{}dimensional strong\char45{}convexity window, its imported arbitrary\char45{}randomized exact lower bound gives the optimization term \$\textbackslash{}sqrt\textbackslash{}kappa S\$; the rare\char45{}event construction gives the statistical term \$V\$. Their maximum is equivalent, up to constants, to \$\textbackslash{}sqrt\textbackslash{}kappa S+V\$. This supports expected loss and fixed\char45{}confidence loss at \$\textbackslash{}delta=1/4\$, without changing the original dimension or accuracy conditions.

For a globally \$\textbackslash{}mu\$\char45{}strongly convex, \$\textbackslash{}beta\$\char45{}smooth objective with initial gap \$\textbackslash{}Delta\$, set \$R\_0=\textbackslash{}sqrt\{2\textbackslash{}Delta/\textbackslash{}mu\}\$. Run the cited high\char45{}probability algorithm at accuracy \$\textbackslash{}epsilon/2\$ and failure rate \$\textbackslash{}delta=\textbackslash{}epsilon/(32\textbackslash{}kappa\textbackslash{}Delta)\$. Its successful event includes output in \$B(x\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star,2R\_0)\$.

Replace outputs outside \$B(x\_0,3R\_0)\$ by \$x\_0\$. The success event is unchanged. Every retained output is within \$4R\_0\$ of \$x\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star\$, so its gap is at most \$16\textbackslash{}kappa\textbackslash{}Delta\$. Expected gap is therefore at most
\$\textbackslash{}epsilon/2+\textbackslash{}delta16\textbackslash{}kap\allowbreak{}pa\textbackslash{}Delta\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}epsilon\$.
The substituted failure rate creates the recorded logarithm. Deterministic query policies remain deterministic.

At \$\textbackslash{}kappa=1\$, the objective is a known\char45{}curvature quadratic plus an unknown affine term. Averaging \$b\$ noisy gradients at a fixed point and taking the resulting quadratic minimizer gives expected gap at most \$\textbackslash{}sigma\textasciicircum{}2/(2\textbackslash{}mu b)\$. Integer rounding yields \$O(1+\textbackslash{}sigma\textasciicircum{}2/(\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}epsilon))\$ samples.

Native pointer: /proofs/2/body; canonical SHA-256: 9b27c613ba68f953d0cf3b03\allowbreak{}c248dac33e4fb6b6008303b1\allowbreak{}9471ea05549ff829


Use Shamir, arXiv:2609.10874v1, Theorem 1 and its explicit construction (PDF pp.2\char45{}3,7\char45{}9; archived characters 3000\char45{}10000 and 14300\char45{}18100). Fix a sufficiently small universal relative\char45{}residual tolerance delta0 allowed by Theorem 1. Its proof constructs, for every sufficiently large condition parameter k and T=c0*k, hard symmetric A with singular values in [1,k], in dimension n<=D*T\textasciicircum{}2; c0,D are universal and independent of k. T can be rounded down. Success probability 2/3 requires Omega(k) products, even for fully adaptive randomized algorithms with the stated stronger source interface. Normalize the supplied nonzero right\char45{}hand side to norm R: relative residual and query count are invariant under rescaling b and the output. Set q=beta*R\textasciicircum{}2/epsilon, m=min(d,q), k\textasciicircum{}2=a*m, where a>0 is a sufficiently small universal constant. Choose a<=delta0\textasciicircum{}2/8 and small enough that the constructed n<=d for T=floor(c0*k). For large enough m, k meets the theorem threshold. Define f(z)=beta*||Az\char45{}b||\textasciicircum{}2/(2*k\textasciicircum{}2) on the hard coordinates and pad with unused coordinates if n<d. Its Hessian is beta*A\textasciicircum{}2/k\textasciicircum{}2<=beta*I; it is convex and globally beta\char45{}smooth. The minimizer A\textasciicircum{}\{\char45{}1\}b has norm<=R, so the ball optimum is zero. A target gradient is simulated by two source products, Ax and A(Ax\char45{}b), scaled by beta/k\textasciicircum{}2; no values, private information or extra native oracle are supplied. Restricting target queries to the ball only restricts the simulated source algorithm. Projecting a feasible target output onto the hard coordinates preserves the residual implication. Expected gap<=epsilon implies by Markov that P(||Axout\char45{}b||>delta0*R)<\allowbreak{}=2*k\textasciicircum{}2/(q*delta0\textasciicircum{}2)<=1/4\allowbreak{}. This yields success at least 3/4, exceeding the source\char39{}s required 2/3. A target budget B induces at most 2B+1 source queries, conservatively including a final query at an unqueried output. If B were smaller than a universal multiple of k, this would contradict the source construction. Thus B=Omega(sqrt(min(d,q))) for sufficiently large m. For bounded m, the uniform extension follows from at least one necessary call: with zero calls, any feasible output X independent of the objective has, on the admissible affine pair f\_plus/minus(x)=plus/minus M*x\_1, maximum expected gap at least M*R; choose M>epsilon/R. Since bounded sqrt(m) is a universal constant, reducing the universal lower constant proves the displayed bound on the entire fixed target domain. Use the exact\char45{}gradient response law, whose centered alpha\char45{}moment is zero, for every sigma>=0. All initialization and simulation calls are counted. This derivation supplies the min(sqrt(d),sqrt(q)) term only, and supplies no log(2+q) lower bound in fixed dimension.

From the frozen centered conditional moment contract, sigma=0 implies every returned gradient equals f\char39{}(x) almost surely. In d=1 the public ball is [\char45{}R,R]. Query f\char39{}(\char45{}R); if nonnegative, convexity proves \char45{}R is an exact minimizer, so return it. Otherwise query f\char39{}(R); if nonpositive return R, an exact minimizer. These two branches handle unbounded affine slopes without assuming bounded initial gap or bounded gradient. Otherwise the continuous monotone derivative has a zero xstar in (\char45{}R,R). Maintain an interval containing a zero, initially [\char45{}R,R]. Query its midpoint. If its derivative is zero return that midpoint; if negative retain the right half, otherwise retain the left half. After k midpoint queries a zero lies in the retained interval of length 2R*2\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}k). Return its midpoint without another query. Its distance to some zero is at most R*2\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}k). Integrating the beta\char45{}Lipschitz derivative from that zero gives f(xout)\char45{}f(xstar)<=beta*|\allowbreak{}xout\char45{}xstar|\textasciicircum{}2/2<=beta*R\textasciicircum{}\allowbreak{}2*4\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}k)/2. Take k=max(0,ceil(log\_4(beta*\allowbreak{}R\textasciicircum{}2/(2*epsilon)))). At most 2+k native gradient samples suffice. All points and the output are feasible, and no function values or certificate are used. The cap is pathwise even on zero\char45{}probability erroneous transcripts: stop after k midpoint steps and output the maintained interval midpoint. Hence the almost\char45{}sure loss guarantee implies the required expected loss for every admissible response law. Randomized algorithms may use this same deterministic algorithm. No hidden constant depends on dimension, precision, beta, R, sigma, mu or Delta.
